summary: KS3 pupils apply formal written methods for all four operations across integers (including negatives), decimals, and proper/improper fractions and mixed numbers. The central difficulty is not any single algorithm but keeping them apart: students (and even some teachers) confuse the procedures — importing addition's common-denominator step into multiplication, or leaving a denominator unchanged in multiplication. Add negative-sign handling and the standard step of converting mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing, since working on the mixed form directly is only correct if every part is fully distributed. Teach by contrasting the four operations on the SAME operands so pupils see when a common denominator is needed and when it is not, always estimating for reasonableness.
misconceptions: Applies the wrong algorithm for the operation — finds a common denominator to multiply, or multiplies across to add
Leaves the denominator unchanged in multiplication, or seeks a common denominator in multiplication/division
Sign errors with negatives (e.g. −5 + 3 treated as −(5+3), or confusing −×− with −+−)
Multiplies or divides mixed numbers without first converting to improper fractions (distributes incompletely)

activities.title: Same two fractions, four operations
steps: Fix two operands, e.g. 3/4 and 2/3, and work all four operations on this same pair, writing out each method.
For addition and subtraction, recut both to a common denominator (9/12 and 8/12) before combining: 3/4 + 2/3 = 9/12 + 8/12 = 17/12 = 1 5/12.
For multiplication, multiply across without a common denominator: 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2 — notice a common denominator is NOT needed here.
State out loud or in writing when a common denominator is required and when it is not, and say why (addition combines same-size parts; multiplication scales).
Before each calculation, estimate: should 3/4 + 2/3 be more or less than 1? Check your exact answer agrees.
activities.insight: Whether a common denominator is needed is a structural feature of the OPERATION, not a ritual applied to every fraction calculation: addition/subtraction combine same-size parts (need a common denominator) while multiplication/division scale (do not, in the standard methods).

activities.title: Spot the wrong method
steps: Examine worked examples where an algorithm has been mis-applied: a multiplication where the common denominator was kept (e.g. 9/12 × 8/12 written as 72/12), or an addition done straight across.
Catch the error, name which operation's method was wrongly imported, and redo the calculation correctly.
Match each incorrect worked example to the specific error it contains.
activities.insight: Being able to diagnose a wrongly chosen method gives evidence that the pupil distinguishes the procedures, though it should be confirmed by the pupil producing correct methods; it confronts the exact confusion documented as tripping up students and teachers alike.

activities.title: Signed integers on a number line
steps: Model −5 + 3 as a move of 3 to the right starting from −5, landing at −2.
Answer: is −5 + 3 bigger or smaller than −5, which direction do you move, and why?
Separate 'combining signed quantities' (addition/subtraction) from 'multiplying/dividing signs', stating the rule for each.
Estimate and check: does combining a negative with a positive of smaller magnitude (e.g. −5 + 3) stay negative?
activities.insight: Adding a positive to a negative moves right along the number line, toward zero and past it if the positive has the larger magnitude (e.g. −5 + 8 = 3); the sign is not simply inherited and magnitudes are not simply summed. Combining signed quantities is a different process from multiplying/dividing signs.

activities.title: Convert mixed numbers before × and ÷
steps: Rewrite a mixed number as an improper fraction before multiplying or dividing, e.g. 2 1/2 = 5/2.
Divide: 2 1/2 ÷ 1/2 by working from the improper form 5/2 ÷ 1/2.
Keep the meaning of division attached — for example reading a division as 'how many halves fit?' — and check the answer makes sense.
Estimate first so an incomplete distribution (multiplying only the whole part) is caught.
activities.insight: Converting mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing is the standard, reliable method; working on the mixed form directly often leads to incomplete distribution (e.g. operating on only the whole part) unless every part is distributed.

checkQuestion: Work these out, showing your method for each: (a) 3/4 + 2/3; (b) 3/4 × 2/3; (c) −5 + 3.
